juce::String Class Referencefinal

## Detailed Description

The JUCE [String](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html "The JUCE String class!") class!

Using a reference-counted internal representation, these strings are fast and efficient, and there are methods to do just about any operation you'll ever dream of.

See also[StringArray](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1StringArray.html "A special array for holding a list of strings."), [StringPairArray](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1StringPairArray.html "A container for holding a set of strings which are keyed by another string.")

## [◆](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html\#ad9d9d48a574f853db4a026bfbeda1b75)CharPointerType

|     |
| --- |
| using [juce::String::CharPointerType](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html#ad9d9d48a574f853db4a026bfbeda1b75) = [CharPointer\_UTF8](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1CharPointer__UTF8.html) |

This is the character encoding type used internally to store the string.

By setting the value of JUCE\_STRING\_UTF\_TYPE to 8, 16, or 32, you can change the internal storage format of the [String](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html "The JUCE String class!") class. UTF-8 uses the least space (if your strings contain few extended characters), but call operator\[\] involves iterating the string to find the required index. UTF-32 provides instant random access to its characters, but uses 4 bytes per character to store them. UTF-16 uses more space than UTF-8 and is also slow to index, but is the native wchar\_t format used in Windows.

It doesn't matter too much which format you pick, because the [toUTF8()](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html#ae032b3196445dc52141644df09e97c74 "Returns a pointer to a UTF-8 version of this string."), [toUTF16()](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html#a224d718b1de795bf9ca44db04d9a6331 "Returns a pointer to a UTF-16 version of this string.") and [toUTF32()](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html#af8e8f0332853454e463b184e61719b32 "Returns a pointer to a UTF-32 version of this string.") methods let you access the string's content in any of the other formats.

("my utf8 string.")). It's _highly_ recommended that you use UTF-8 with escape characters in your source code to represent extended characters, because there's no other way to represent unicode strings in a way that isn't dependent on the compiler, source code editor and platform.

Returns the character at this index in the string.

In a release build, no checks are made to see if the index is within a valid range, so be careful! In a debug build, the index is checked and an assertion fires if it's out-of-range.

Also beware that depending on the encoding format that the string is using internally, this method may execute in either O(1) or O(n) time, so be careful when using it in your algorithms. If you're scanning through a string to inspect its characters, you should never use this operator for random access, it's far more efficient to call [getCharPointer()](https://docs.juce.com/master/classjuce_1_1String.html#a00c64666a3b7ecd084665773ff8dbb53 "Returns the character pointer currently being used to store this string.") to return a pointer, and then to use that to iterate the string.

String str = ...;

// BEST
for (auto c : str)
    DBG (c);

// GOOD
for (auto ptr = str.begin(), end = str.end(); ptr != end; ++ptr)
    DBG (*ptr);

std::for_each (str.begin(), str.end(), [] (juce_wchar c) { DBG (c); });

Although the string's contents won't be affected by this call, it will increase the amount of memory allocated internally for the string to grow into.

juce::String Class Referencefinal

Detailed Description

The JUCE String class!

Using a reference-counted internal representation, these strings are fast and efficient, and there are methods to do just about any operation you'll ever dream of.

See also
StringArray, StringPairArray

◆ CharPointerType

using juce::String::CharPointerType = CharPointer_UTF8

This is the character encoding type used internally to store the string.

By setting the value of JUCE_STRING_UTF_TYPE to 8, 16, or 32, you can change the internal storage format of the String class. UTF-8 uses the least space (if your strings contain few extended characters), but call operator[] involves iterating the string to find the required index. UTF-32 provides instant random access to its characters, but uses 4 bytes per character to store them. UTF-16 uses more space than UTF-8 and is also slow to index, but is the native wchar_t format used in Windows.

It doesn't matter too much which format you pick, because the toUTF8(), toUTF16() and toUTF32() methods let you access the string's content in any of the other formats.
